kill_argument: The pre-specified H1 verdict ('not supported') rests on one state's data break, and the remaining post hoc evidence cannot tell a referee whether the first stage is real. Remove Georgia's six L tests and the H1 critical value drops from 3.45 to t at nu (1.76), and every H1 statistic exceeds it. But the selected DDT candidate's 2014-2019 wage gap drifts by about 0.055 over the post window against an ATT of 0.092, and that segment holds California's own 2016-2019 minimum-wage ramp. A paper whose first stage is 'not supported, possibly because of Georgia, possibly real, possibly trend' does not license any reading of the H2 employment result as the effect of a binding wage floor. That is a scope limit, not a defect the crew can still fix. What I attacked and found holding: r-ph-h1-joint states both checks, both caveats and the verdict, and its numbers match the run metrics. D7 now matches runs/posthoc/run.json (unreviewed, with the human's agreement) and discloses the defective flags. No run was added or replaced, no label changed, and validate passes with the three known paper warnings. What remains is two wording gaps in the cross-references (R12, R13).

findings.text: H1's verdict, and everything that follows from it, is set by Georgia alone. The H1 critical values come from the decision-set L quantile (crit_h1_hi95 = 3.449 and crit_h1_hi975 = 4.320, both from_L = 1; t_nu = 1.758 and 2.139). In runs/level-mde/tests.csv the top four of the 60 L wage t-values are Georgia at 2016Q1-2016Q4 (4.54, 4.32, 3.45, 3.31). The other nine L states have max 1.13, and Georgia itself gives -0.35 and 0.11 at 2017Q1-Q2. In data/derived/state_panel_pre.csv Georgia's 722513 average weekly wage is 287-304 in 2014 (above California's) and 255-276 in 2015. Its year-over-year log change, measured against the cross-state median, is -0.150 to -0.170 in 2015Q1-Q4. That is the largest break in the panel (the next is FL 2018Q4 at -0.078), and the employment series shows no break. That pattern fits a reporting or classification change (not verified). The DDT trend over B'-8..B' straddles the break exactly at the pseudo-dates 2016Q1-2016Q4 and not after it. Without Georgia's six values, the L q95 and q975 are 0.75 and 0.76, so c_hi = t_nu. Then the pooled H1 (t 2.66), year 1 (2.04) and year 2 (2.99) all reject, and the 95% interval lower end is about +0.018. My computation from the run outputs; report-only, not a proposed verdict. The same quantile sets MDE_h1 = 0.148, the anticipation wage interval's lower end (c_hi975 = 4.32), the 'not computed' elasticities and 'H2 uninformative about the wage floor'. runs/NOTES.md item 5 notes the surprise but does not trace it, and no claim mentions it. The verdict follows the pre-specified rule and should stand, but as worded r-v-h1, r-v-h2-note and r-h1-wage-h1-c-hi95 invite the reading 'no detectable first stage', which the run outputs do not support.

Remedy (cheapest; verdict unchanged): add text claims, backed by level-mde, saying that the H1 critical values come from Georgia's four 2016 pseudo-date tests and that the remaining L values never exceed t_nu. Qualify r-v-h1 and r-v-h2-note to 'not supported at the pre-specified L-calibrated critical value'. Put h1_p_upper_tnu next to it. The paper must not say the wage floor had no detectable effect on weekly earnings. A report-only check of Georgia's 2014-2015 722513 wage series against the BLS county files or the QCEW notes would show whether it is an artifact. Any new metric needs a code review round before it runs.

findings.text: The H2 label was effectively decided before any post-period data were read, and the contribution statement cannot survive it. level-mde gives prob(inconclusive) = 0.95 at tau = 0 and 0.829 at tau = -0.035, and prob('smaller than 2%') = 0 under both. h90_h2 = 0.054 > b = 0.02 and MDE_h2 = 0.092, 2.6 times the CEM estimate the bound is meant to test; with the real SE, h2-emp gives 0.107 and 0.063. California's own six H2 placebo t-values have RMS k = 0.37: the max SE is about 2.7 times the spread of California's pseudo-ATTs, so the width comes from the conservative SE, not from noise observed for California. Both published readings (CEM about -3.5%, Dube about 0) lie well inside the 95% CI [-0.106, 0.047]. Yet plan.json contribution still says 'H2 adds an equivalence test against a 2% bound that separates the two published readings', and the H2 text says a CI inside +/-0.02 excludes CEM's median estimates. That outcome had probability 0. The claims are correct as numbers. The finding is scope: 'inconclusive' is the expected outcome under either reading, and the Writer will draft from a contribution sentence the results contradict.

State the label probabilities (already claimed) and k_h2 next to the headline label. Do not describe the result as evidence against either published estimate.

The pre-registered H2 hypothesis text is left as registered, which is correct.

findings.text: The out-of-fit pre-period evidence the design names for DDT is not in the claims. identifying_assumption (ii) says the seven 2022Q1-2023Q3 event-path gaps are DDT's trend fit points (curvature only) and that 'DDT's out-of-fit pre-period evidence is the 2014-2019 segment of the path'. The claims report only the in-fit segment: RMS 0.006 and 0 bands excluding 0. In runs/event-path/event_path.csv the 2014-2019 detrended employment gap rises steadily from -0.045 (2014Q1) to -0.002 (2019Q4), an OLS slope of 0.0023 per quarter. The wage gap rises from -0.245 to -0.044, 0.0085 per quarter. So the relative trend fitted on 2022Q1-2023Q3 (seven post-COVID quarters, extrapolated up to ten quarters) is not the 2014-2019 trend. At the post window's mean horizon of 6.5 quarters the gap in slopes is about 0.015 log points for employment (three-quarters of b) and about 0.055 for wages (60% of the H1 estimate). The bands are wide (SE 0.07-0.15), so no single quarter 'fails'. But a claim set showing only the in-fit RMS reads as a pre-trend pass that the design itself says it is not.
findings.evidence: runs/event-path/event_path.csv rows quarter 2014Q1-2019Q4, outcomes emp and wage; runs/event-path/metrics.json (no 2014-2019 metric); plan.json design.identifying_assumption (ii), design.method ESTIMATORS DDT (7 trend points for the real B, 9 at pseudo-dates); claims r-event-emp-2022q1-2023q3-rms-gap, r-event-case. Remedy: report the 2014-2019 segment as DDT's out-of-fit evidence, either as a report-only metric (slope or RMS of the 2014-2019 detrended gap) added to event_path.py, which needs a code review before it runs, or in the fig-event caption and a text claim. Add a limitation: the DDT counterfactual extrapolates a seven-quarter post-COVID trend that differs from the 2014-2019 one.
findings.response: Not a claim fix: code/posthoc.py part (c) reports the 2014-2019 out-of-fit slope per quarter of the employment and wage event-path gaps and their implied size over the post window, after its code review; the limitation goes to the Writer.
findings.ruling: runs/posthoc part (c) reports the 2014-2019 out-of-fit evidence and it is claimed: r-ph-emp-slope-2014-2019 0.0023/q, r-ph-wage-slope-2014-2019 0.0085/q, implied post-window sizes 0.0149 and 0.055, RMS 0.032 and 0.141, end-point gaps. I recomputed the wage slope from runs/event-path/event_path.csv (0.00847/q). The limitation sentence is left to the Writer, which is acceptable at this stage; how these numbers must be read next to the posthoc Georgia check is R9.

findings.text: S2 (Dube SDID) fails California's own pre-period level check, yet its interval will stand in the abstract next to the primary. California's six S2 pseudo-ATTs are all positive, +0.024 to +0.034 (mean about +0.029, larger than b), with t from 1.55 to 2.12. k_s2_se = 1.86, and California's one-sided upper rejection rate is 4 of 6 (3 of 6 at t_nu) even with the max SE and the SDID floor. S2's 95% interval [-0.047, 0.028] is the narrowest of the three, and its reused-weights wage interval [0.035, 0.116] excludes 0. Both come from the procedure whose pre-period behaviour for California is worst. The label ('inconclusive') is not wrong. The risk is reading S2's narrower interval as support for a near-zero effect, or as an independent confirmation of the first stage in R1.

findings.text: The plc-nonff qualifier does not give the direction. California's employment outside 722513 ran +2.45% above the counterfactual (95% CI [0.003, 0.046]), the same size as |H2|. If the same California-wide deviation reached 722513, the H2 estimate is biased toward zero or positive, not toward a decline. 'Not separable from a California-wide shock' leaves the reader to guess.

findings.text: The fit numbers hide bias. The selected candidate's six pseudo-ATTs are all positive (0.0001 to 0.0154, mean 0.010), so most of the selection RMSE of 0.0112 is a systematic shortfall of the counterfactual, not noise. On wages the same estimator gives California's six pseudo-ATTs all negative (-0.014 to -0.062, mean -0.032, RMS about 0.036, above b). H1 inherits an estimator chosen on employment that fits California's wages poorly before the policy. California's H1 pseudo-ATTs are not claimed; only H2's and S2's are.

findings.text: The Ferman-Pinto A + B/pop diagnostic is degenerate for the post-period statistics: h2_fp_a = -0.00043 with h2_fp_se = 0.0, and likewise h1_y1, h3_y1 and h3_y2 (fp_a < 0, fp_se = 0). These are unclaimed, but the California pseudo-date FP diagnostics are claimed (r-ca-*-fpa/fpb/fpse). An SE of 0 must not appear as a standard error. Report the diagnostic only as evidence that the A + B/pop fit fails here, which supports the max-SE choice.

findings.text: The two post hoc checks of D7 point in opposite directions on H1, and no claim puts them together, so each invites a one-sided reading the evidence does not support. Part (b) yields about 30 claims (r-ph-gal-*, r-ph-galnu-*) saying that with Georgia's six L tests removed the pooled, year-1 and year-2 H1 t-values exceed c_hi(0.95) = t_nu and the pooled 95% interval is [0.018, 0.166]. Part (c), claimed separately (r-ph-wage-slope-2014-2019, r-ph-wage-implied-post), says the selected DDT candidate's 2014-2019 wage gap drifts at 0.0085 per quarter, 0.055 log points over the post window's mean horizon, against an H1 ATT of 0.092 with SE 0.0346 (runs/h1-wage/metrics.json). Read alone, (b) says 'the first stage is there once a Georgia artifact is removed'; read alone, (c) says 'most of the wage effect is trend drift' (0.092 - 0.055 = 0.037, t about 1.07 at the same SE, below t_nu; my arithmetic from the claimed numbers, not a test). Neither is right. Against (c): the event-path wage gap steps from 0.005 (2024Q1) to 0.076 (2024Q2), about 2.3 times the largest quarter-to-quarter change in 2014-2019 (0.030; runs/event-path/event_path.csv), which a linear drift does not produce, and the 2014-2019 segment contains California's own general minimum-wage ramp (T17, stated in r-ca-h1-* texts), so which relative trend applies after 2023Q3 is not identified. Against (b): it removes one state chosen after seeing the results. The paper stage is when the abstract and introduction get written from these claims, so the joint reading has to be fixed now.

Remedy (cheapest; no new run): one text claim backed by posthoc b_gaL_h1_t_exceeds_chi95, c_wage_implied_post and h1-wage h1_att stating that both checks are post hoc, that they pull in opposite directions, that neither changes the pre-specified verdict, and that the paper may cite neither without the other. Optionally a text note on the 2024Q1 -> 2024Q2 step, backed by event-path, as descriptive context only.

findings.text: The posthoc run's own outputs contradict a claim. runs/posthoc/metrics.json has b_loo_<fips>_changes_chi = 1 for all ten L states, b_loo_n_changing = 10 and b_loo_changing_states listing all ten, and runs/posthoc/stdout.log prints 'leave-one-out changes c_hi for 01,13,18,22,37,42,45,47,48,55'. Claim r-ph-loo-only-georgia says only Georgia's removal moves c_hi. The claim is right: I checked the values, and the nine non-Georgia c_hi(0.95) differ from the pre-specified 3.4487049201 by 9.4e-10 and c_hi(0.975) by 6.0e-10, within the stated 1e-9 (tests.csv stores T inputs at %.10g; the flags use 1e-12). runs/NOTES.md discloses the defect and the flags are unclaimed. But the clean rerun the submission gate needs will reproduce the wrong flags and the wrong stdout line, and a replicator reading metrics.json will see '10 changing'.

findings.text: The 'cite both or neither' cross-reference reaches only 3 of the 51 claims backed by part (b) metrics (2 of the 24 r-ph-gal-* and r-ph-galnu-* claims, plus r-h1-crit-georgia), and misses the most quotable ones. r-h1-crit-georgia, r-ph-gal-h1-exceeds and r-ph-galnu-h1-exceeds carry it, but r-ph-gal-h1-lo95 (0.018) / -hi95 (0.166), r-ph-galnu-h1-lo95 (0.019) / -hi95, the year-1 and year-2 exceeds claims (r-ph-gal-h1-y1-exceeds, -y2-exceeds and the galnu pair, all value 1) and their intervals (y2 lower ends 0.029 and 0.030), and r-ph-gal-crit-hi95/hi975 do not. On the drift side, r-ph-wage-rms-2014-2019 (0.141) and the end-point gaps (-0.245 to -0.044) do not either. findings.text: The employment drift claims point to the wrong joint reading. r-ph-emp-slope-2014-2019 (0.0023/q) and r-ph-emp-implied-post (0.0149) now say 'Read together with r-ph-h1-joint: the paper may not cite this post hoc check without the other one', but r-ph-h1-joint is about H1 wages only and names no employment counterpart, so 'the other one' has no referent for H2. The employment drift bears on H2: extrapolated, it implies about +0.015 of the -0.029 H2 estimate (runs/h2-emp/metrics.json h2_att), which would move H2 toward a larger decline. That is the same direction as r-plc-nonff-sign (H2 biased toward zero or positive). No claim states this direction, so a reader can take the drift only as a doubt about the wage effect. The H2 label is 'inconclusive' either way, so nothing changes in the verdict.
